House in committee on Bill (No. 115) respecting the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.-Mr. L. G. McCarthy.

I notice the promoter of this Bill is not here. I do not think we can go on with these Bills without the promoter. If we are to pursue that course how will we get members to attend the House. If members wish to have legislation put through they must be present.

I do not think the objection is well taken because according to the rule if the member who is in charge of the Bill, or whose name appears on the back of it is not present some other member may move in his name. I do not think the point of order is well taken.

I am not rising to a point of order ; I am reasoning the matter. I take the ground that members should be here. We sit here day after day almost without a quorum and members have put their names on the back of Bills as a guarantee of their genuineness. Then they go away and remayi at home, they do not come here to attend to their legislation and a few members who do attend are expected to assume the responsibility of putting that legislation through. So long as we continue doing that we will find that members will absent themselves. They get their matters put through whether they are here or not, and I think it is time the House took a stand and said no Bill should be proceeded with at any stage in the House unless the member who has charge of it is present to vouch for its bona tides. This Bill is reported as amended ; we have not the printed amendments before us and we want somebody here to explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can give all the explanations or they can be given by anybody who was present in the committee.

The Minister of Justice is very kind, but that does not get over the difficulty that he has only half a quorum behind him. I think the minister should join with us in adopting some measure that will act as an' incentive to members to be present at the sittings of the House to attend to the legislation. I raise the question not as a point of order but as something that should guide us with a view to having the affairs of the House conducted-I shall not say with propriety because we do that at all times-but in a proper way. A member in charge of a Bill asks the House to put through a certain measure and he ought
to be here to explain any clauses of it and to show by his presence that he has sufficient interest in the Bill to ask the House to put it through. I appeal to the House to endorse me on this question because I think it is the proper stand to take. I do not ask you to rule, I am not aware that there is any rule to prevent the Bill going on but I think as a matter of policy the House should say : We will allow the Bill to stand until the member is present.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the best policy at this stage of the session is to expedite the Bills and get on so that we will get home at some time between this and December.

What do you think of the importance of a Bill when the promoter is not here ? The Minister of Justice says that this Bill was discussed in committee, but it does seem to me that when the promoter of the Bill has not enough interest in it to be present the legislation in his judgment cannot be very important. I certainly think the House should sustain the position taken by the member for Halton (Mr. Henderson).

It has come to this in this House now that if a few members who are in the liabit of attending regularly were to vacate their seats for a few hours we would have no session, and I think the privileges accorded to members are being abused to the fullest extent. It is a disgrace and a shame and if members who are occupying seats in this House cannot attend sometimes they had better resign and let others take their seats who will attend. It is certainly going beyond all decency to say the least. There are members who would like to take an hour off but who are compelled to sit here day after day because the other members will not attend.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (for the Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: I explained this item before six o'clock.
This is a very large sum of money.
It is the usual vote.

No, for the Department of Public Works. My hon. friend knows that there are a number of officers with special technical knowledge whose salaries are paid out of this vote.
This is the usual vote and is intended to provide for the payment for technical works for the use of engineers, architects and draughtsmen.

Yes.

. Mr. BRODEUR. Many of these are periodical publications and also technical works necessary for the use of officers of the department.

To provide for expenditure in connection with Transportation Commission, $15,000.

This is to provide for the remuneration of the commissioners, travelling expenses, salaries of two secretaries, and scientific and expert professional assistance necessary in connection with the commission's investigations.
This does not pay the salaries of the commissioners ?
Yes ; the commissioners are paid $25 a day.
When they travel ?
Yes.
When they do not travel they do not get anything ?
No.
What have these gentlemen done ?

They have made a couftle of reports. But I must say that wu have been somewhat unfortunate in connection with this commission. Sir Wm. Van Horne, who was first offered the chairmanship, xvas unable to accept the position. Then Mr. John Bertram, who was made chairman, suffered a lingering illness which resulted in his death. And Mr. Reford a member of ihe commission met with an accident which prevented him from taking part in the work of the commission.

I think I have heard everything the minister has now said three times already this session. Before we vote more money for this Transportation Commission, I must ask that some more definite statement be made as to what they have done, what they are doing, when they are likely to complete their labour and what the result of it all is expected to be. I have already brought the matter to the attention of the House on two different occasions and have asked that we be given something more than the vague statements which we have heard three times already and which amount to just nothing at all. This commission was constituted in 1903, and from that time to the present I do not know one single matter in which it has been of the slightest assistance to parliament, although during that interval we have dealt with many important matters in transportation. We have been voting money year after year, and we do not know whether the men sitting there are constituted as a commission at the present time, who are the members of it, what it is doing, or anything at all about it. I would like the minister to make a full, definite and clear statement as to these matters, about which I have asked twice already during the present session, or else let this item stand until the government is prepared to make that statement. I think the Minister of Inland Revenue will realize that I am not asking anything unreasonable.
I have no objection to let the item stand.
And I trust the hon. gentleman will take what I have said as notice that we do expect a statement on this matter.
I do not know whether the leader of the opposition remembers that an interim report has been laid before the House some time ago, with regard to the port of St. John.
It was an interim report with regard to some feature of one port.

But he must admit that there have been many accidents. Lately the secretary of the commission became paralyzed. Some gentlemen who were appointed did not accept the position, and most of those who were appointed have either died or retired for one reason of another.

Whose logs are going down in such great quantities ?
The logs of the lumber merchants.
Are we paid for the logs that go through our booms ?
Yes ; and we are paid by Messrs. Gilmour & Hughson.

As I understand, the government has a series of booms and slides in the river, and where this particular boom or slide is situated they make use of it as if they owned it, and inasmuch as they get compensation for the use of all these slides and booms they pay this amount to certain persons whose work has done a certain part of the service. It may be that apart from this work the lumbermen have to make provision for running their logs down the streams which lead into the Ottawa.
